opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that the world doesn't hand you problems in the shape your training distribution expected. If you want a system that's reliable across arbitrary domains and over long horizons, you need it to be able to stop, think, check its work, and recover when something goes wrong. That is fundamentally what inference-time compute buys you.

If you look at a pure forward pass, the model gets one shot. It has a fixed amount of computation per token, and whatever it produces, it produces. That's fine for a lot of short tasks. But when you chain together hundreds or thousands of steps, as you do in a real long-horizon task, small per-step error rates compound really quickly. Ninety-nine percent per-step accuracy sounds great until you realize that over a few hundred steps you're almost guaranteed to fail somewhere. So you can't get to reliability just by making each individual step marginally better. You need a mechanism for noticing mistakes and correcting them, and that requires spending more compute at the moment you're actually solving the problem.

My background is in game-playing AI, poker in particular, and I think that experience is really instructive here. The big leaps in systems like Libratus and Pluribus, and in AlphaGo on the Go side, didn't just come from a better policy network. They came from search, from spending compute at decision time to look ahead, consider alternatives, and refine the plan for the specific situation in front of you. A raw policy is a great prior, but planning on top of it gets you much stronger and more robust behavior, especially in situations the policy didn't see much of during training.

The challenge, and why this is hard in general domains, is that games give you a perfect simulator and a clean reward. In the real world you don't have that. You have to figure out how to verify, how to evaluate intermediate states, and how to decide when you're done. A lot of what I think matters now is building systems that can do that kind of self-verification and course correction in messy, open-ended environments, whether that's research, coding, or any multi-step task where you can't just check the answer at the end.

So for me, inference-time compute isn't a nice-to-have optimization. It's the thing that lets you trade extra thinking for extra reliability, and reliability over long horizons is exactly what you need if you want these systems to actually do meaningful work autonomously rather than being clever autocomplete.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fixed computation per token and spending more compute while solving, but does not say that complex tasks require different amounts of deliberation for different tokens.

r002.rationale: It identifies verification, evaluation, and knowing when to stop as challenges, but does not identify finding productive ways to spend vastly more inference-time computation on an individual token as a major unresolved challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is: pre-training gives you a model that is right most of the time, and "most of the time" is exactly what breaks over long horizons.

Think about what a long-horizon task actually is. It's not one hard decision, it's a chain of hundreds or thousands of small ones, and the errors compound. If each step is ninety-nine percent reliable, after a few hundred steps you're basically flipping a coin on whether the whole thing succeeds. You can't close that gap purely by making the base model a bit smarter, because the marginal gains from scaling pre-training are real but they're incremental, and the reliability requirement is exponential in the length of the task.

Inference-time compute changes the shape of that problem. Instead of asking the model to get every step right in a single forward pass, you let it think: generate candidates, check them, notice when something doesn't add up, back up, try again. That's what humans do. Nobody writes a large piece of software or solves a hard research problem by emitting the answer token by token with no revision. The reason people are reliable on long tasks isn't that their first instinct is always right, it's that they have a loop of verification and correction sitting on top of their intuition.

And crucially, this is what makes it general-domain rather than narrow. In games like poker, we knew for years that search at decision time was worth an enormous amount, but that search was hand-engineered for one environment. What's different now is that the model itself is the search operator. It proposes, it critiques, it decides where to spend more effort, and it does that in natural language across any domain where it has some ability to judge its own work. So the same mechanism that lets it be careful on a math proof lets it be careful on debugging a codebase or planning a multi-week project.

There's also a very practical argument. Inference-time compute is adjustable. For an easy question you spend a little, for a problem that really matters you spend a lot, and you can push reliability up by paying more rather than waiting for the next training run. That gives you a dial on correctness, and reliability is ultimately what makes these systems usable for real work instead of impressive demos.

So I'd put it this way: pre-training determines how good the model's instincts are, and inference-time compute determines how far you can trust those instincts to carry you before the chain breaks. For long-horizon autonomy, the second one is the bottleneck.

r001.rationale: The response says inference effort can vary by problem and that the model can decide where to spend more effort, but it does not state that deliberation should vary across individual tokens.

r002.rationale: The response presents adjustable inference-time compute as a practical benefit, but does not identify productively spending vastly more computation on a single token as a major unresolved challenge.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that different problems require very different amounts of computation. If you ask a simple factual question, you want an answer immediately. If you ask a model to solve a difficult problem or carry out a project with hundreds of steps, you want it to be able to spend more time reasoning, checking its work, and revising its approach.

That matters for long-horizon reliability because small errors compound. Even if each individual step is usually correct, a sufficiently long sequence can still fail. So you need more than a model that makes a good first guess. You need a process that can notice when something went wrong, test assumptions, and recover. Inference-time compute gives you room to do that.

The challenge is making that extra computation useful across domains. Generating more text doesn't automatically make an answer more reliable. The model has to know what to check, when to use a tool, and whether the evidence actually supports moving forward. So I see inference-time compute as an important ingredient: it lets the system allocate effort to the difficulty of the task, including the effort needed to catch its own mistakes.

r002.rationale: It describes making extra computation useful as a challenge, but does not identify vastly more inference-time computation on an individual token as the unresolved challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that different problems require very different amounts of thought. If you want a system to work reliably across a broad range of tasks, it needs the ability to spend more computation when something is difficult—to explore alternatives, check its assumptions, and revise a plan when it finds a mistake.

That becomes especially important over long horizons. A small error early on can send you down the wrong path, and if you just keep executing, you compound it. You want the system to periodically ask: Am I actually making progress? Does this result support the next step? Should I go back and try something else?

But more inference-time compute isn’t automatically more reliability. If the model spends longer reinforcing the same mistaken assumption, that doesn’t help. You need training that teaches it to use that computation productively, and ideally feedback from the environment so it can distinguish a plausible answer from something that actually works. The important capability is allocating effort, checking progress, and recovering from mistakes.
